summary: Tomas Marrow, the night baker, makes four small loaves while steady rain falls on Harbor Lane. He tidies, waits, and dozes by the warm oven as the lighthouse beam passes the window.

description_summary: A slow night shift at a small seaside bakery, told gently over steady rain, with ambience after the story so you can stay asleep.

Deep navy and teal shadows, a single warm light source, no faces, no religious buildings or symbols.

script:
Hello, and welcome back to Fernwick.

[pause]

Tonight it is early October, and a steady rain is falling on the harbor. It has been falling since the afternoon, soft and even, the kind of rain that asks nothing of anyone. On Harbor Lane the shop windows are glowing amber, and in one of them, the bakery called Marrow and Crumb, the night baker is just beginning his work. Nothing much is going to happen tonight. That is the whole plan.

[pause]

Let yourself get comfortable now. Let your shoulders drop, and let your hands rest wherever they like. Take one slow breath in, and let it go. Take another, a little slower. You don't need to remember anything from today, and you don't need to stay awake for the ending. The story will be perfectly happy without you. If you drift off in the middle, the rain will keep going, and so will the baker.

[long pause]

At eleven o'clock, Tomas Marrow unlocks the back door of the bakery and steps inside, shaking the rain from his coat. He is a large man, and a quiet one, and he moves through the dark kitchen the way you move through your own house at night, without needing to look. He hangs the coat on its hook. He switches on one lamp above the long wooden table, and the room fills with a low, golden light.

[pause]

The kitchen smells of yesterday's bread and warm stone. It is a comforting smell, a little sweet, a little like toast. On the shelf above the sink sits a small radio, and Tomas turns it on so softly that it is only a murmur, a slow piano playing something old. He has never once turned it up. He says the bread likes it this way.

[pause]

Pip is already there. Nobody has ever seen Pip arrive. The cat is simply curled on a folded flour sack beside the big oven, eyes half closed, as if she has been waiting there since the beginning of time. Tomas nods to her. She doesn't nod back, which is how they both like it.

[pause]

First, the oven. He opens the iron door and checks the coals, and then he adds one small log, and then he closes the door again. A faint orange glow shows through the crack at the bottom. The warmth begins to spread across the floor, slowly, until even the corners of the kitchen feel soft.

[pause]

Next, the flour. He fills a wooden scoop from the big bin and tips it into the wide bowl, and then another scoop, and then another. The flour makes a soft sound, like a sigh, each time it lands. A little cloud rises and hangs in the lamplight, and settles again on the table, on his sleeves, on the tip of Pip's tail. Pip does not mind. Pip is asleep now.

[pause]

Water from the copper jug, warm but not hot. A pinch of salt. A spoon of the starter, which lives in a crock by the window and has been alive longer than anyone on Harbor Lane can remember. Tomas lifts the cloth from the crock and looks at it kindly. "Good evening," he says, in a voice barely louder than the radio. "Rain tonight. You'll like that."

[pause]

Then he puts both hands into the bowl, and the real work begins. It is slow work. He folds the dough over itself, pushes it away with the heel of his hand, turns it a quarter turn, and folds it again. Fold, push, turn. Fold, push, turn. The rhythm is as steady as the rain on the window, and after a while the two sounds become hard to tell apart.

[pause]

Outside, the rain keeps falling on the harbor. It drums gently on the awning, runs down the glass in thin bright lines, and drips from the gutter into a puddle by the step. Somewhere out past the breakwater a buoy rocks on the water and gives one soft, far-off note, and then, a long while later, another.

[pause]

When the dough is smooth, Tomas shapes it into a round, covers it with a cloth, and sets it on the shelf above the oven to rest. "Take your time," he tells it. Then he pulls up the tall wooden stool, sits down, and pours himself a cup of tea from the pot that has been keeping warm on the back of the stove. He holds the cup in both hands. Steam curls up and disappears.

[pause]

This is the best part of the night, and Tomas knows it. There is nothing to do but wait. The dough is rising. The oven is warming. The rain is falling. Every few minutes, a slow beam of pale light sweeps across the bakery window and moves on. It comes from the lighthouse at the north point, where Oriel Penhallow is polishing the brass lens in slow circles, humming a tune that doesn't quite have an end. Tomas lifts a hand to the window each time the light passes. He is not sure Oriel can see him. It doesn't matter.

[pause]

While he waits, he tidies the way he always does. He wipes the table with a damp cloth and hangs it over the edge of the sink. He lines up the wooden spoons by size. He turns the labels on the jars so they all face the same way, honey, caraway, oats, and dried apple. Nobody will notice, but Tomas will, and that is enough.

[pause]

After an hour, he lifts the cloth from the dough. It has grown round and plump, soft as a pillow. He divides it into four, shapes each piece into a loaf, and lays them in a row on the long board. Four small loaves, side by side, like sleepers in a train carriage. He cuts one gentle line across each, slides the board into the oven, and closes the door.

[pause]

Now the smell begins. Warm. Toasty. A little like honey. It drifts through the kitchen and under the front door and into the lane, where the rain carries it a little way and then lets it go. A cat on a windowsill two doors down lifts her head, sniffs, and puts it back down.

[pause]

Tomas sits again, and the tea is still warm. His eyelids are heavy. He lets them close for a moment, only a moment, and listens. The oven ticks as it heats. The radio plays its low piano. The rain taps. The cat breathes, slow and even. Everything in the room is doing exactly what it should, and so there is nothing left for him to do.

[pause]

When the loaves are done, they sound hollow if you tap them, like a small, soft drum. He lifts them out one at a time and sets them on the rack by the window to cool. Steam rises from them in the lamplight. The rain on the glass has slowed to a gentle patter. Morning is still hours away.

[long pause]

Tomas turns down the lamp. He rests his arms on the table, beside the warm bread, and lays his head down. The kitchen is quiet. Pip stretches one paw and curls it back. The beam from the lighthouse passes once more across the window, and moves on.

[long pause]

And the baker sleeps.

[long pause]

[[SECOND]]

Let's tell it once more, a little slower.

[long pause]

It is early October in Fernwick. Rain is falling on the harbor.

[long pause]

Tomas unlocks the bakery door and comes in out of the rain. He turns on one lamp. The kitchen is warm, and it smells of bread.

[long pause]

Pip is curled on a flour sack by the oven. She is already asleep.

[long pause]

Tomas puts a log in the oven. He tips flour into a bowl. He adds warm water, a pinch of salt, and a spoon of starter. "Good evening," he says.

[long pause]

He folds the dough. Pushes. Turns. Folds. Pushes. Turns. The rain taps the window in the same slow time.

[long pause]

The dough rests. Tomas sits with his tea. A pale light sweeps across the window, and moves on.

[long pause]

Four small loaves go into the oven. The kitchen smells of honey and toast.

[long pause]

The bread comes out, and cools by the window. The rain is soft now.

[long pause]

Tomas lowers the lamp. He rests his head on his arms. Pip sleeps. The rain goes on.

[long pause]

The lamps are low in Fernwick. Sleep well.
